audience.programmeDescription: English Language and Culture at the University of Amsterdam studies English-language literature and the history, structure and use of English. This example follows English Linguistics and Literature.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines literary and language study. Other options focus on world literatures and adaptation or on language and public culture. UvA offers dedicated sequences in English linguistics and literary history and requires a thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The literacy diagnostic and study tutoring carry no credits.

componentNotes.uva-elc-y1-ling1: UvA studies the social history of English and the structure of words.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y1-ling2: UvA studies the spread of English and how it varies around the world.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y1-ling4: UvA teaches methods for collecting and analysing language data. UCR offers general research methods.

componentNotes.uva-elc-y2-ling5: This example studies how English varies across communities and social settings.

componentNotes.uva-elc-y2-programme-electives: Students choose 12 EC from approved English Language and Culture options.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y2-free: Students have 12 EC of free electives in year two.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y3-philosophy: UvA examines how researchers produce knowledge in the humanities.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y3-debates: UvA examines current debates in English linguistics and literary studies.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y3-seminar: The research seminar develops the topic and methods for the thesis.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y3-free: Students have 30 EC of free electives in year three.
componentNotes.uva-elc-y3-thesis: UvA requires a thesis after the research seminar. UCR independent research is optional.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

GOSHIST112.name: Histories of Gender
GOSHIST112.text: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

GOSSOCI212.text: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

GOSSOCI214.text: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.text: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

HCBCOGN311.name: Higher Order Functions
HCBCOGN311.text: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. Topics include attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

HCBGATE102.text: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

HCBPSYC111.text: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

HCBPSYC313.text: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.text: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.text: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.

MCCCOMM312.text: Creative Communication Laboratory combines close reading and creative workshops with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop traditional or hybrid creative projects grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.text: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM312.text: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.text: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
